title: Noah builds (Genesis 6–7)
hookLine: a righteous man builds a boat under a clear sky

cards: A man in a quiet neighborhood starts building a boat in his backyard. Not a canoe: a ship longer than a football field, three decks high, nowhere near any water. Day after day, the sound of saws, for years.
The well-known retellings of Noah are full of mocking crowds, jokes and a lonely builder. Genesis never mentions a single neighbor's reaction. Not one word.
What it gives us instead is a man, an instruction, and a long, plain list of measurements.

teach.b: First, the world. By chapter six, the story says the earth is corrupt and filled with violence, and God is grieved at heart. Cain's one murder has become a whole culture.

In the Douay-Rheims: "Noe was a just and perfect man in his generations, he walked with God." Noe is the old Latin spelling of Noah, and walked with God is the same phrase Genesis used for Enoch. Third, the instruction.
God tells him to make an ark of timber planks, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high, roughly four hundred fifty feet, with rooms, a window and a door in the side.

teach.h: TEVAH: A SHIP AND A BASKET.
teach.b: The Hebrew word for ark, tevah, appears in only one other story in the Bible: the little basket the baby Moses floats in on the Nile.
A giant ship and a reed basket, the same word, each carrying someone through the water to a new beginning.
Fourth, what Noah does, the whole point of the chapter: "And Noe did all things which God commanded him." Genesis says it more than once. No speech, no argument.
He builds. Then the rain comes, forty days and forty nights, and the ark lifts off the ground. From early on, Christians read the ark as more than a boat.

The First Letter of Peter compares the flood waters to baptism, and Church Fathers saw the ark as the Church, carrying people safely through. The flood is still named in the Easter Vigil's blessing of the baptismal water.
A man building under a clear sky, because he trusted the one who told him to.

how: At the Easter Vigil, the priest's blessing of the baptismal water recalls the flood as a sign of baptism, and Catholics have long pictured the Church as an ark.

games.q: you're Noah. God tells you to build a ship three hundred cubits long, with no flood anywhere in sight. what does the text say you do?
o: ask God for a sign first.
warn the neighbors and wait to see.
games.why: "And Noe did all things which God commanded him." Genesis gives no speech and no argument. he builds.

practice: Think of a good thing you've put off because it looks odd or too slow to matter: writing to someone who never writes back, saving for something far away, going to Mass alone, practicing an instrument nobody hears.
Let the reasons not to come up and pass, and picture laying its first plank. If you pray, ask for Noah's kind of steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Noah builds. A just man who walked with God, building an ark with no water in sight, and doing all things God commanded him.

orig.note: Hebrew: ark, box. used only for Noah's ark and the basket of the infant Moses.

carryVoice: Your line: build anyway. The plans come first; the rain comes later. Until tomorrow, then.
